title: Incident-ready network hardening guide — private deployments
summary: Working guide for making private deployment VPCs "incident-ready": hardening patterns, firewall rule templates, mTLS placement, RBAC v2 to network mapping, audit log schema for evidence, and automated SIEM export/playbooks.
body:
Purpose:
Provide a compact, operational guide engineers can use during onboarding, audits, and incident response to ensure a private deployment meets our compliance and uptime goals. This is purposely utilitarian: checklists, minimal config snippets, and automated evidence packaging steps.

Scope and constraints:
- Applies to Redwood Private (VPC & on-prem) but focuses on VPC-hosted private deployments.
- Target audience: infra engineers, SREs, security engineers, and solutions engineers supporting customers.
- Goal: produce deterministic evidence artifacts for audits and reduce ad-hoc ticket chasing during incidents.

Quick decision map (when an incident hits):
1) Is there active data exfiltration suspected? -> escalate to incident commander and enable egress-deny override.
2) Is control plane connectivity affected? -> switch to fail-open gold path to maintain telemetry and evidence export.
3) If forensics needed: snapshot SGs, flow logs, and TLS session history (see Evidence section).

Operational priorities:
- Keep latency and observability measurable during hardening.
- Automate evidence collection with signed, immutable archives.
- Map RBAC roles to network policy changes so approvals are auditable.

Notes to reviewers:
- This doc is intentionally prescriptive where possible; policy language is provided as examples rather than final configs.
- Feedback requested on retention periods for flow logs (30d vs 90d) and on the choice of hash algorithm for chain-of-custody (sha256 recommended).
vpc_and_topology_patterns:
Recommended VPC patterns:

1) Transit-proxied customer model:
- Customer VPC -> VPC Peering/Transit Gateway -> Redwood Transit VPC -> Service subnets.
- Benefits: central firewalling, single egress inspection point, consistent mTLS termination decisions.
- Tradeoffs: single point for operational changes; ensure redundant control plane paths.

2) Single-tenant-per-az subnets for high sensitivity workloads:
- Each tenant has isolated subnets, Egress NAT per-tenant, and dedicated SGs.
- Benefits: easier evidence scoping and quicker per-tenant forensics.

3) Hybrid on-prem breakouts:
- On-prem customers use VPN/Direct Connect into a transit VPC with strict route-table controls.
- Ensure control-plane endpoints are only reachable from whitelisted customer networks when required.

Design rules:
- Minimal public surface: only management bastions and LB frontends as needed.
- Zero-trust egress defaults: deny by default; use allow-lists for approved destinations.
- Centralized DHCP and DNS logging (cloud-native resolver logs or BIND audit).
firewall_and_network_rules:
Firewall rule template (example):

- Name: allow-controlplane-ingress
- Direction: ingress
- Source: 10.0.0.0/16, CUSTOMER-CIDR (if admin)
- Protocols: tcp:22, tcp:443, tcp:8123 (control plane agent)
- Action: allow
- Logging: enabled -> export to audit-bucket/flow-logs/%Y-%m-%d

Egress restrictive example:
- Name: tenant-egress-allow-list
- Direction: egress
- Source: 10.10.0.0/24 (tenant subnet)
- Destinations: 10.20.0.0/24 (internal services), 52.95.0.0/16 (approved external APIs)
- Ports: tcp:443
- Action: allow
- Implicit default: deny

Microsegmentation guidance:
- Use SGs for coarse controls; use host-level policies (e.g., Calico or Cilium) for pod/process-level segmentation.
- Enforce service-to-service mTLS for any east-west traffic across tenants.

Operational checklist for rule changes:
- Author -> Reviewer (network lead) -> Automated test in staging -> Rollout to canary -> Full rollout.
- All steps must create audit entries with change ID linked to RBAC v2 approval (see RBAC mapping field).
mtls_and_certificate_management:
mTLS placement and lifecycle:

Where to terminate mTLS:
- Control-plane: terminate at ingress proxies inside the transit VPC to centralize cert validation.
- Data-plane (east-west): prefer end-to-end mTLS between services, with tiered trust (service CA signed leaf certs).

Certificate issuance flow:
- Authority: customer-managed CA or Redwood-managed private CA (per contract).
- Issuance: cert-manager (k8s) or Vault PKI with short-lived certs (recommended: 1h-24h TTL for service certs).
- Rotation: automated, overlapping validity windows, preflight verification.

Example envoy snippet (conceptual, not deploy-ready):
cluster:
  name: backend_service
  connect_timeout: 0.25s
  tls_context:
    common_tls_context:
      tls_certificates:
        - certificate_chain: /etc/envoy/ssl/tls.crt
          private_key: /etc/envoy/ssl/tls.key
      validation_context:
        trusted_ca: /etc/envoy/ssl/ca.crt
        verify_subject_alt_name: [ 'spiffe://redwood/tenant/*' ]

mTLS hardening checklist:
- Disable legacy TLS versions <1.2 on all proxies.
- Reject connections without valid client certs at the proxy for privileged endpoints.
- Log certificate subject and SANs as part of session records (see audit schema).
rbac_v2_mapping:
RBAC v2 -> network operations mapping (operational table):

Roles and network permissions:
- network-admin: can create/modify firewall rules, change route tables, manage transit attachments.
- deployment-operator: can request temporary network exception requests (timeboxed) and perform canary changes with network-admin approval.
- auditor: read-only access to flow logs, packet captures, policy history, and audit archives.

Approval flow examples:
- Any firewall rule that relaxes egress defaults requires: request ticket -> deployment-operator request + network-admin approval -> automated test -> timestamped audit record with approver id and change diff.

Enforcement pattern:
- All RBAC changes must create an immutable audit entry including change_id, actor (id), role, justification, and linked evidence archive URL.
- Map roles to short-lived API tokens bound to specific network change endpoints.

Operational note: integrate RBAC v2 with SSO (OIDC) so audit logs contain OIDC subject and email; avoid service-account-only approvals for high-privilege network changes.
audit_log_schema:
Canonical audit log JSON line (each record is a single JSON object, newline-delimited logs):

{
  "timestamp": "2026-03-08T14:23:01Z",
  "tenant_id": "tenant-1234",
  "deployment_id": "dpl-78",
  "actor_id": "aisha.patel@redwood.com",
  "action": "firewall.rule.change",
  "change_id": "chg-20260308-0007",
  "details": "allow egress tcp:443 to 52.95.0.0/16 for service analytics",
  "src_ip": "10.10.5.22",
  "dst_ip": "52.95.10.9",
  "protocol": "tcp",
  "port": 443,
  "verdict": "allowed",
  "cert_subject": "CN=svc-analytics,OU=tenant-1234",
  "trace_id": "trace-abc123",
  "evidence_url": "s3://redwood-evidence/tenant-1234/chg-20260308-0007.tar.gz"
}

Fields to prioritize in SIEM: timestamp, tenant_id, action, change_id, actor_id, src_ip, dst_ip, verdict, trace_id, evidence_url. Include JSON schema validation in pipeline to drop malformed entries.
siem_export_instructions:
SIEM export recommendations:

1) Ship audit JSON lines directly to SIEM ingestion (preferred) via a secure forwarder (Fluentd/Vector) with TLS and mTLS towards SIEM collectors.
2) Enrich records: add geo-ip for external destinations, ASN, and risk-scoring tag (low/medium/high) prior to indexing.
3) Map fields in Splunk/Elastic:
   - event.time -> timestamp
   - user.name -> actor_id
   - network.src_ip -> src_ip
   - network.dst_ip -> dst_ip
   - network.transport -> protocol
   - network.port -> port
   - redwood.change_id -> change_id

Log retention guidance:
- Operational logs: 90 days hot, 1 year warm.
- Audit/evidence bundles (signed): 7 years (or customer-specific contract retention).

Example Vector config fragment (conceptual):
[sources.file]
  type = "file"
  include = ["/var/log/redwood/audit/*.jsonl"]

[sinks.siem]
  type = "http"
  inputs = ["file"]
  uri = "https://siem-collector.example.com/ingest"
  encoding = "json"
  auth.strategy = "mutual_tls"

Operational note: ensure your SIEM ingest has idempotency keys (use change_id + file checksum) to avoid duplicate evidence indexing.
evidence_automation_steps:
Automated evidence packaging (recommended daily + on-demand):

1) Gather sources:
   - VPC flow logs for the affected period (cloud provider API)
   - Audit JSON lines for RBAC and firewall changes
   - TLS session metadata (cert subject, fingerprint, duration) from ingress proxies
   - Packet capture snippet (pcap) if packet-level forensics required (timebox to 2-5 minutes for privacy)

2) Normalize and sign:
   - Normalize filenames: tenantid_YYYYMMDD_HHMMSS_{artifact_type}.jsonl
   - Create a manifest.jsonl listing artifacts with sha256 sums
   - Create a tar.gz of artifacts and sign with a dedicated evidence signing key (use Vault transit sign)

3) Store and publish:
   - Push to customer-specific S3/GCS bucket with server-side encryption and object lock enabled when required
   - Publish an index record to the audit index with evidence_url, signer, signature, and retention policy

4) Chain-of-custody record:
   - Each package must include signer id, sign timestamp, and a verification instruction (how to re-hash and verify signature).

Example minimal packaging script (conceptual):
#!/bin/bash
set -e
OUT=tenant-1234_20260308_1423
mkdir -p /tmp/$OUT
cp /var/log/redwood/audit/*.jsonl /tmp/$OUT/
cp /var/log/aws/vpcflow/*.log /tmp/$OUT/
sha256sum /tmp/$OUT/* > /tmp/$OUT/manifest.sha256
# sign manifest via vault (placeholder)
# vault write transit/sign/evidence key=manifest.sha256 -> signature
tar -czf /tmp/$OUT.tar.gz -C /tmp $OUT
# upload to s3 with server-side encryption
# aws s3 cp /tmp/$OUT.tar.gz s3://redwood-evidence/tenant-1234/ --storage-class STANDARD
ascii_diagram:
Customer VPC
   |
   | (VPN/DirectConnect)
   v
  [Transit VPC - central firewall & ingress proxies]
   |    \
   |     \ (mTLS validated)
   v      \
  [Redwood Control Plane endpoints]   [Service subnets - private]

Notes: keep at least two independent paths from customer networks to transit VPC for redundancy. Log all ingress proxies and ensure they forward certificate metadata to audit logs.
hardening_checklist:
- [ ] Default egress deny on tenant subnets
- [ ] Central transit firewall with logging enabled and daily automated export
- [ ] mTLS enforced for control-plane agents and for east-west traffic where possible
- [ ] Certs issued via short-lived PKI and auto-rotated
- [ ] RBAC v2 integration with SSO and auditable approvals for network changes
- [ ] Daily evidence packaging job configured and monitored
- [ ] SIEM pipeline validates JSON schema and enriches records
- [ ] Immutable audit archives with retention policy configured per contract
- [ ] Playbook for incident evidence collection tested quarterly
- [ ] Automated tests that simulate firewall rule changes in staging prior to production rollout
open_questions:
- Do we standardize on 30d or 90d VPC flow log hot retention by default?
- Should evidence signing use customer-provided keys for some regulatory customers?
- How long should short-lived service cert TTLs be for high-churn services (1h vs 6h)?
- Can we add an automated verifier that runs weekly to check signature validity across the evidence bucket?
